Before bringing to life the NetStim Lab in April 2019, Andreas worked as a postdoc at the Laboratory for Brain Network Imaging and Modulation headed by Prof. Michael Fox at Harvard. Prior to that, he completed an MD/PhD with Prof. Andrea Kühn in the Movement Disorders and Neuromodulation Section at Charité Berlin, conjointly with a scientific appointment at the laboratory of Prof. Felix Blankenburg (Bernstein Center for Computational Neuroscience / Max Planck Institute for Human Development). Andreas also holds a Dr. med., which he obtained under the guidance of Prof. Cornelius Weiller in Freiburg. As a PI he is affiliated with the PhD program of the Einstein Center for Neurosciences Berlin and the International Graduate Program Medical Neurosciences at Charité Berlin, and teaches medical as well as postgraduate-level courses.

Within the scope of his scientific work, Andreas is keenly interested in the interactions between the basal ganglia and the cerebral cortex. Phylogenetically, both originate from the peduncular hypothalamus and form a system optimized in controlling our environment, first and foremost by means of action (e.g., motor output). Hence, Andreas strives to explore network connectivity and causality in this system, the human connectome and its structure-function relationship. As a clinical case of connectomics, he studies effects of deep brain stimulation (DBS) on aberrant circuitries that lead to movement disorders. These interests are often realized by furthering development of the Lead-DBS toolbox, which Andreas envisions as a collaborative platform for the refinement and scientific application of methods to study how DBS interacts with the brain.

When not in the lab, Andreas may be found marveling at the invigorating powers of the coffee machine in the kitchen or hidden in the lab’s cooler eating ice cream. He may (or may not) have played in dubious rock bands with doubtful musical output back in the days, but nonetheless his love for music has lived on until today. Apart from that, Andreas also has a thing for podcasts (he even hosts one himself – it’s called Stimulating Brains !) and the ramblings of Jerome Salinger, whom he credits as his favorite author. Ningfei Li gave him a drone once, which is amazing, but if you see Andy and his drone you better watch out because he has only been crashing into trees with it so far.

Aysu is an MD/PhD student at NetStim, Berlin since October 2022. She has a PhD fellowship from Einstein Center of Neurosciences, where she also is a student representative. In 2025, she moved to Cologne to continue her research as a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Cologne, employed by the Uniklinik Köln.

During her medical studies at Hacettepe University, Turkey, she was fascinated by the complexity of the human brain and amazed by the avenues that medical imaging has created. Her broad interests include movement disorders and connectomics. She believes in the value of neuromodulation in improving patients’ lives as well as its potential to shed light onto disease mechanisms. Her current project focuses on understanding the connections responsible for clinical improvement after deep brain stimulation for Tourette’s syndrome across different targets.

After her PhD, she wants to continue her career in medicine and become a clinician scientist who is equipped with computational tools to tackle clinical questions. Brainstorming and problem solving as a team are highlights of being a scientist for her. She is passionate about high quality education and would like to improve as a teacher along her PhD. In her free time, she enjoys rock climbing and even more to cheer on climbing friends from a hammock. She is interested in art and is currently trying to learn how to draw.

Patricia joined the Netstim lab as a fast-track PhD student in October 2022, supported by the Einstein Center for Neuroscience fellowship. At the time, she was completing her MSc degree in Medical Neurosciences at Charité, while already working on her PhD project. She also holds a BSc (Hons) degree in Neuroscience, which she earned at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. In 2025, she moved to Cologne to continue her research as a postdoctoral fellow at the University of Cologne, employed by the Uniklinik Köln.

Patricia’s research interests primarily focus on understanding and developing methods for analysing neuroimaging data. Recently, she also discovered a passion for coding. Currently, she is investigating the extent to which neuroimaging data can explain variance in clinical improvement of patients after Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS). Specifically, she is working with a sample of Parkinson’s disease patients. Her second project includes exploring the ways by which we can improve the way we study brain functional connectivity. What she enjoys the most about academia is the opportunity to delve into the knowledge that no one else might have learned before, and that there is always an opportunity to learn something new.

Beyond her academic interests, Patricia enjoys reading, playing the guitar, painting, hiking, and powerlifting (a random mix of hobbies in no particular order). As a child, her favourite book was an encyclopedia of dog breeds. Feel free to quiz her on this topic – she loves dogs.

Pepsi joined the NetStim Lab in April 2026 as a Mental Health Coach and Senior Scientist. While her formal background remains largely undocumented, her recent behavior suggests considerable expertise in selective obedience and subtle emotional influence. Her primary research interests focus on the processing of complex sensory information within the olfactory system, as well as the activation of the nucleus accumbens. She regards with particular emphasis the temporal dynamics of reward processing, most notably when induced by treats. Moreover, she is currently conducting an observational study investigating whether the mere act of watching a door influences its likelihood of opening more quickly. Preliminary results were, as expected, highly promising and have been submitted to Nature , pending peer review and sufficient treat-based funding. Outside of her scientific endeavors, Pepsi is known for her remarkable stage presence. Acting as an unofficial double of Shakira, she demonstrates exceptional hip movements and vocal expression.
Maike joined the Netstim Lab in 2025 as a postdoctoral researcher at Uniklinik Köln.

Adriana joined the Netstim Lab in 2025 as a PhD student at the University of Cologne, working at Uniklinik Köln. With a Bachelor’s and a Master’s degree in Bioengineering from the Faculty of Engineering of the University of Porto, she is driven by a strong passion for developing impactful technologies that improve quality of life and advance healthcare provision.

Her research focuses on personalized modeling of basal ganglia circuitry and on understanding how individual brain connectivity can explain variability in motor outcomes following deep brain stimulation.

Beyond her enthusiasm for exploration and learning in research, Adriana enjoys physical exercise and the quiet pleasure of a well-read book, finds renewal in nature, and believes that karaoke or a good laugh with friends remains one of life’s most reliable forms of therapy.
Christine joined the Netstim Lab in 2025 as a PhD student, working jointly between the University of Cologne and Forschungszentrum Jülich.

Ellen joined the NetStim lab in 2026 as a postdoctoral researcher, working across the Departments of Functional and Stereotactic Neurosurgery and Neuropediatrics at the Uniklinik Köln. She holds a BPsych(Hons) and PhD in Neuroscience from Deakin University in Melbourne, Australia.

Ellen’s research interests include identifying disease-related brain networks and optimising therapeutic brain stimulation, particularly in relation movement disorders. Her current project focuses on analysing deep brain stimulation (DBS) electrode placements for childhood dystonia, with the aim of improving treatment outcomes for patients with cerebral palsy and other dystonia-related conditions.
Outside research, Ellen is excited to travel and enjoy exploring her new surroundings in Germany.
Jan Philipp joined the NetStim lab in 2026 as a postdoctoral researcher, working in the Departments of Functional and Stereotactic Neurosurgery at the Uniklinik Köln.

Frauke joined the NetStim Lab in 2026 as the administrative executive, working at Uniklinik Köln. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Literary and Linguistic Studies from RWTH Aachen University and is also a Certified Foreign Language Correspondent in English. After working as a research assistant at RWTH centralized Biomaterial Bank Aachen and Schneider C. Lab (Gastroenterology) at Uniklinik Aachen for almost 3,5 years and completing interdisciplinary modules in Neurolinguistics and Neuropsychology as part of her course of studies, she is looking forward to the upcoming years at NetStim Lab.

When Frauke is not busy writing e-mails and maintaining office operations, she enjoys reading a good book, exploring the outdoors with her dog Nils – a Corgi-Jack Russell Terrier Mix – and learning new languages. Recently, she is trying to pick up Italian again, which she started learning back in High School. If you want to really get her talking, ask her about Doctor Who. She’s been a Whovian for nearly two decades and it’s her comfort show.

Lara joined the NetStim lab in March 2026 for a research rotation and her Master’s thesis as part of her M.Sc. in Clinical and Experimental Neurosciences at the University of Cologne. She previously obtained her Bachelor’s degree in Psychology (cum laude) from Radboud University in the Netherlands. Her research interests lie in neurological and psychiatric disorders and how neural networks differ between healthy and pathological states. She plans to pursue a PhD in Neuroscience, after completing her Master’s degree. In her free time, she can often be found (not entirely successfully) trying to relearn French, enjoying dinner parties with friends, or watching handball. She enjoys exploring new sports places and appreciates a good espresso – occasionally in the form of an espresso martini.

Richard joined the NetStim Lab in November 2025. He is a medical student at the University of Cologne and previously spent time in labs at TU Munich, UCSF, and the Mayo Clinic. Outside the lab, he enjoys reading, podcasts, and good food, and is slowly being buried by his ever-growing mountain of Anki reviews.

Benjamin joined the NetStim Lab as a postdoctoral researcher in January 2026. He initially studied biomedical engineering for a few semesters before switching to psychology. During the five years he lived in the Netherlands, he completed a Bachelor of Science in Psychology at Radboud University and the Donders Institute in Nijmegen, and a Master of Science at the University of Groningen. He then worked as a neuropsychologist in the Department of Neurology at the University Hospital Göttingen, before moving to the University Hospital Bonn, where he became involved in developing and evaluating digital therapeutic methods for mental disorders and in non-invasive brain stimulation. In 2024, he received his PhD in Medical Psychology from the University of Bonn.

At the Institute for Network Stimulation, his research is supported by DFG funding, giving him the opportunity to focus on his main area of interest, the development of personalized protocols in TMS. He is interested in how individualized brain mapping and circuit dynamics can guide stimulation targeting and improve treatment response. Benjamin has played tennis since the age of four, competed in teams for years and trained as a coach, though he makes it onto the court only occasionally these days. He also enjoys reading other than scientific articles, or listening to audiobooks and podcasts. He particularly enjoys traveling to France and generally to the sea. Occasionally, he tries to recall his childhood piano lessons, only to give up in frustration.

Michael joined the NetStim Lab in July 2026.
Helen is an MD student who joined the lab in Boston in April 2023, where she focuses on her MD thesis project aimed at creating a detailed brain atlas for DBS imaging.

Her journey into medicine began with a foundation in psychology, where her work with neuropsychiatric patients sparked a profound interest in neurology and functional neuroanatomy. This experience led her to explore imaging research with the goal to bridge clinical practice with scientific inquiry. In her bachelor’s thesis, she used fMRI and eye-tracking to probe brain networks involved in social attention.

Working with neuropsychiatric patients was a key motivator in her decision to transition into medical school. She pursues an additional degree in translational medicine to lay the foundation for a clinician-scientist career. Her favorite topics are anatomy and intensive care medicine.
Helen is excited to immerse in Boston’s academic environment and is committed to making a meaningful contribution to the field through her atlas project.
Beyond her interest in the brain, Helen is passionate about interior design and loves spending time in the mountains, either hiking or skiing.
